case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
case.limits: The court leaned on the shooter's independent criminal act as a superseding cause. A system that interacts, personalises and responds in the moment is harder to cast as inert media, and current cases are testing precisely that seam.
case.holding: Makers of video games and films owed no duty of care for a school shooting allegedly influenced by their content, the crime was not sufficiently foreseeable, and intangible media content is not a product for strict liability.
case.why_ai_cites_it: The media-violence litigation of the 1990s produced the defense playbook now reused for AI harms: no duty to unforeseeable victims of a user's acts, superseding criminal conduct, and content-is-not-a-product. Chatbot harm suits are answered with this case's structure almost paragraph for paragraph.

reading.body:
The Sixth Circuit's 2002 ruling in *James v. Meow Media* is the template for how AI companies currently defend against harm claims: no duty to unforeseeable victims, the user's independent act as a superseding cause, and the position that content is not a product subject to strict liability.

The court held that video game and film makers owed no duty of care for a school shooting allegedly influenced by their content, because the violence was not sufficiently foreseeable and because intangible media cannot be treated as a defective product. Those three holdings translate almost directly into the defense structure appearing in AI harm litigation today. When a chatbot interaction is alleged to have contributed to injury, defendants reach for foreseeability arguments, superseding-cause arguments, and content-is-not-a-product arguments in the same sequence the Sixth Circuit used here.

The data identifies four live cases against Character Technologies that cite this precedent, all testing the same doctrinal seam. The court's own reasoning flagged where that seam is weakest: a system that personalises and responds in the moment is harder to characterize as inert media than a film or a game with fixed content. Whether real-time, individualized AI output survives the *James* framework is precisely what those four cases are now deciding. This record covers duty and foreseeability doctrine only; it does not address how courts may treat the compute infrastructure or training choices behind such systems.

section.name: AI Case Law: The Precedents Behind the Defenses
